aiOverview.content: A pied-à-terre (French for "foot on the ground") is a small second home, apartment, or condominium, typically located in a major city, that is used for part-time, temporary, or seasonal residence rather than as a primary, year-round home. While often associated with the wealthy, these units serve as convenient, low-maintenance urban bases for commuters, frequent travelers, or those who enjoy a city lifestyle without living there full-time.Key Characteristics and UsageDefinition: It is a secondary residence that is not the owner's primary address.Purpose: Used for work-week stays, short-term visits, or to avoid long commutes.Location: Often found in high-end urban neighborhoods.Real Estate Context: In cities like New York, condos are generally more flexible with pied-à-terre usage, while co-ops may restrict or prohibit them.Pied-à-terre in NYC Real Estate (Current Developments)As of April 2026, New York State officials are negotiating a "pied-à-terre tax" as part of the state budget to help close a projected $5.4 billion budget deficit.Tax Proposal: Governor Hochul and city officials are proposing a yearly surcharge on residential properties worth $5 million or more that are not used as a primary residence.Target: The tax primarily targets non-residents, international buyers, or wealthy individuals who use luxury condos as occasional homes.Impact: The tax is intended to generate roughly $500 million annually.OriginsThe term originated in the 18th century, referring to soldiers who would dismount their horses ("mettre pied à terre") to occupy temporary lodging. A pied-à-terre (French for "foot on the ground") is a small second home, apartment, or condominium, typically located in a major city, that is used for part-time, temporary, or seasonal residence rather than as a primary, year-round home. While often associated with the wealthy, these units serve as convenient, low-maintenance urban bases for commuters, frequent travelers, or those who enjoy a city lifestyle without living there full-time. Key Characteristics and Usage Definition: It is a secondary residence that is not the owner's primary address. Purpose: Used for work-week stays, short-term visits, or to avoid long commutes. Location: Often found in high-end urban neighborhoods. Real Estate Context: In cities like New York, condos are generally more flexible with pied-à-terre usage, while co-ops may restrict or prohibit them. Pied-à-terre in NYC Real Estate (Current Developments)As of April 2026, New York State officials are negotiating a "pied-à-terre tax" as part of the state budget to help close a projected $5.4 billion budget deficit. Tax Proposal: Governor Hochul and city officials are proposing a yearly surcharge on residential properties worth $5 million or more that are not used as a primary residence. Target: The tax primarily targets non-residents, international buyers, or wealthy individuals who use luxury condos as occasional homes. Impact: The tax is intended to generate roughly $500 million annually. OriginsThe term originated in the 18th century, referring to soldiers who would dismount their horses ("mettre pied à terre") to occupy temporary lodging.
